question: Can the fragmented attention-sink literature be given a coherent cross-architecture definition and taxonomy that distinguishes how sinks are utilized, mechanistically interpreted, and mitigated, and can that synthesis support practical choices for training, tuning, efficient inference, interpretability, hallucination reduction, robustness, long context, and multimodal systems?

key_findings.claim: The survey defines an attention sink by a conjunction, not by high attention alone: a token must receive exceptionally large attention while contributing little semantic or task information.
key_findings.evidence: The text operationalizes numerical extremeness with cumulative received attention above tau times the global mean, citing tau=1000 from prior work, and separately classifies low-information token types such as special markers, initial delimiters, and background patches. It also repeats a cited observation that the first token is the maximum-attended token in 98% of heads for selected LLMs. None of these thresholds or semantic labels is newly validated by the survey, and the cumulative statistic is not normalized for context length, layer, or head composition.

anchors.section: 2.2.2 Attention Sink: Extreme Attention Concentration on Uninformative Tokens, Equation 5

key_findings.claim: The paper broadens the attention-sink object far beyond the original causal-LLM first-token pattern, but the included phenomena have materially different locations, dynamics, and functions.
key_findings.evidence: The survey describes fixed [CLS]/[SEP] bands in encoder-only language models; first-token, delimiter, and weak-semantic sinks in causal LLMs; SuperExpert-linked sinks in MoE LLMs; scattered visual-background sinks in multimodal models and ViTs; middle-layer, globally semantic sink registers in diffusion transformers; and moving rather than initial sinks in diffusion language models. This is useful scope expansion, but it is evidence for a family resemblance rather than one validated invariant mechanism.

key_findings.claim: Fundamental utilization is organized into four intervention roles: preserve naturally occurring sink tokens, redistribute their attention, insert learnable prefix sinks, or repurpose sink properties for another objective.
key_findings.evidence: The four branches are distinguished as passive retention, active mass reallocation, proactive trainable absorption or aggregation, and task-specific reuse. The synthesis maps preservation to streaming/KV compression/sparse attention/quantization, redistribution especially to multimodal grounding and calibration, learned prefixes to registers and information bottlenecks, and repurposing to attack, defense, and efficient selection. Equations 13-39 provide canonical abstractions, but they are survey-level reformulations rather than a common algorithm tested by the authors.

key_findings.claim: Mechanistic interpretation is usefully separated into mathematical pressure, numerical circuitry, functional bias, representational geometry, and additional training or information-flow theories, but the paper does not establish that these accounts compose into one causal mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: The main branches are Softmax limitations/no-op behavior, aligned weight-activation-attention outlier circuits, nearly input-independent attention-output bias, and geometric anchoring. Additional accounts include causal-mask/RoPE bias, anti-overmixing, spectral energy, active-dormant heads, mix-compress-refine, and outlier-driven rescaling. Evidence ranges from attention/value observations to architecture-changing interventions; no mediation analysis or common experiment tests whether the proposed levels are necessary, sufficient, mutually exclusive, or sequential in the same model.

anchors.section: 4.5 Summary of Interpretations of Attention Sink

key_findings.claim: Mitigation methods are synthesized under two higher-level principles: provide an explicit controllable substitute for an implicit sink, or cut a causal link that produces the sink.
key_findings.evidence: Explicit substitutes include output/value gating, learnable key-value or denominator bias, residual gated rescaling, and architectural isolation. Causal-chain interventions include clipped or non-normalized attention, optimizer/loss/norm changes during pre-training, value-path changes, and tuning regularizers. The survey consistently notes deployment trade-offs: many methods require pre-training from scratch, post-Softmax edits conflict with fused kernels, gates add latency or parameters, and flattening attention may damage tasks that require sharp focus.

key_findings.claim: The only quantitative literature-level synthesis is a cumulative-publication plot reporting growth from 39 to 107 to 186 to 206 papers and a January 2026 split of 106 utilization, 68 interpretation, and 32 mitigation papers.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3 labels totals 39 around October 2023, 107 around October 2024, 186 around October 2025, and 206 in January 2026; the last stacked count is 106+68+32=206. The paper does not state the databases, query strings, screening dates, deduplication rules, multi-label counting policy, coder agreement, or uncertainty behind this trend, so it is a descriptive author tally rather than a reproducible bibliometric analysis.

key_findings.claim: The reported corpus size is internally inconsistent and cannot be reconstructed from the stated method because no review method is stated.
key_findings.evidence: Page 6 says the taxonomy covers over 210 studies, page 7 says over 200, and page 73 says over 180; Figure 3 totals 206. A reviewer count of Appendix A finds 222 table rows but only 208 unique bracketed reference IDs because papers are repeated across architecture groups. The bibliography has 245 entries, many of which are background architecture or method references rather than attention-sink studies. These quantities may reflect different cutoffs or inclusion scopes, but the paper never explains the differences.

key_findings.claim: The universal low-information definition conflicts with several cases that the survey itself treats as sinks but describes as semantic carriers, information bottlenecks, or indispensable functional biases.
key_findings.evidence: Section 2.2 makes limited semantic contribution essential to sink status. In contrast, diffusion-transformer sinks are said to carry global/semantic image information and cause a perceptual shift about six times random masking; register tokens are said to aggregate critical information; VLA register tokens encode dense global spatial context and improve real-world manipulation by 17.1%; and omni-modal sink values organize the representation as a shared bias. The survey needs separate labels for null sinks, semantic hubs, learned registers, and high-attention anchors rather than treating all as one object.

anchors.section: 3.3.2 Vision Artifact Mitigation and Information Aggregation

key_findings.claim: At least one surveyed mathematical formulation is transcribed in a direction that contradicts the described method.
key_findings.evidence: For FOCUS, Equation 31 gives L_sink=||A_[SINK]||_2^2 while calling it an attraction loss that trains the token to absorb attention. Minimizing the displayed positive squared norm would repel attention from the sink. The official FOCUS v2 source instead uses a negative, layer/head-averaged mean attention term, -lambda times mean A_{i,k_sink}, so the survey omits both the negative sign and the actual aggregation. This concrete error cautions against treating the survey's unifying equations as source-faithful implementations.

key_findings.claim: The nine scenario guidelines are an index into the taxonomy, not experimentally validated decision rules.
key_findings.evidence: Sections 6.1-6.9 map papers to pre-training, tuning, efficient inference, mechanism interpretation, hallucination reduction, safety/robustness, general capability, long context, and multimodal enhancement. They do not compare methods under a common model, budget, sink metric, accuracy metric, or deployment constraint, and they do not specify when preserving a functional sink should dominate removing it. Accordingly, the recommendations are useful routing heuristics but not evidence that one branch is best for a scenario.

key_findings.claim: Some deployment claims are stated more strongly than the survey's own caveats allow.
key_findings.evidence: Gated attention is described as adding minimal computational overhead on page 56, while the field-level challenge section says gating introduces non-negligible latency, especially for element-wise variants. Modified Softmax is called simple and architecture-agnostic on page 60, yet the same discussion and page 71 warn that it normally requires retraining and may be incompatible with optimized attention kernels. These are design-dependent trade-offs, not generally resolved properties.

key_findings.claim: The survey's 'attention redistribution' branch is not internally closed under its own mass-preservation definition: it mixes redistribution with post-Softmax deletion and wholesale head-pattern replacement.
key_findings.evidence: Page 25 defines redistribution as moving freed sink mass to targets while preserving total mass and makes Equation 20 require alpha+beta=1. Yet page 27's 'sink reduction' sets alpha<1 and beta=0 while leaving every non-sink entry unchanged. For a normalized attention row its new sum is 1-(1-alpha) times the original sink mass, which is below one whenever a nonzero sink is attenuated; this is output attenuation or gating, not redistribution. Equation 23 then copies the densest sink head's complete pattern to other heads, replacing rather than reallocating their token mass. The same page calls Softmax 'zero-sum,' although its relevant invariant is sum-to-one. These are taxonomy and terminology defects, independent of whether the cited methods are useful.

anchors.section: 3.2 Attention Redistribution and 3.2.1 Core Methodology, Equation 20
3.2.2 Sink reduction and attention-sink-pattern broadcasting, Equations 22-24

key_findings.claim: This is a narrative survey with no new controlled experiment, theorem, pooled effect estimate, or formal evidence-quality assessment.
key_findings.evidence: The contribution section describes taxonomy, methodological synthesis, future directions, and scenario mapping; the body restates equations and selected results from cited papers; Appendix A supplies tags, venue, year, and links. There is no review-method section, search flow, inclusion/exclusion protocol, risk-of-bias assessment, or independent replication. The author limitation section only acknowledges incomplete coverage of emerging architectures, not these methodological limits.

method.core_idea: Construct a cross-architecture narrative map of attention sinks, first defining the object and cataloguing its manifestations, then coding prior work by utilization, mechanistic interpretation, mitigation strategy, and application scenario.
method.mechanism: The survey uses a hierarchy rather than a new model: PDF pp.8-20 Section 2 separates manifestations in classical LMs, dense and MoE LLMs, multimodal LLMs, ViTs, DiTs, and other transformers; p.21 Section 3 defines four utilization roles; pp.36-52 Section 4 groups explanations into four named core mechanisms plus additional theories; pp.53-67 Section 5 groups interventions into four named mitigation families plus additional techniques and then reduces them to explicit-substitute versus causal-chain strategies; and pp.68-70 Section 6 maps work to nine application scenarios. Canonical equations abstract representative techniques, p.6 Figure 3 gives a publication tally, and pp.74-85 Appendix A tag the cited studies.
assumptions: A token's semantic or task information can be judged reliably from its token type, position, or visual location without a standardized causal contribution test.

First-token concentration, BERT special-token attention, high-norm ViT background artifacts, DiT semantic registers, multimodal visual hubs, and moving diffusion-LM sinks share enough structure to support one attention-sink label.
Attention probability is meaningful evidence of token importance even though the survey also emphasizes that value norms and final A-times-V contributions can be small.
The threshold statistic in Equation 5 transfers across sequence lengths, layers, heads, architectures, and modalities despite using a global cumulative-attention mean and a source-specific tau.
The cited papers' terminology, equations, settings, and results have been transcribed accurately; no source-verification or error-correction protocol is reported.

Heterogeneous metrics such as sink rate, attention share, activation kurtosis, perplexity, quantized accuracy, hallucination score, speed, and qualitative attention maps can support cross-method guidance without pooled normalization.
Softmax no-op pressure, outlier circuits, implicit bias, and geometric anchoring are complementary levels of one story rather than competing explanations that require model-specific adjudication.

Reductions in attention concentration after changing gating, normalization, optimization, or architecture identify the sink as the causal mediator of downstream gains rather than one correlated change among several.
The paper list is sufficiently comprehensive to support a first-survey claim, despite no database search, cutoff, screening, inclusion, deduplication, or coder-agreement protocol.

The temporal category counts in Figure 3 are mutually exclusive and stable enough to describe a field trajectory, even though Appendix A uses multiple labels and repeats papers across architecture groups.
Practical recommendations transfer from the cited model and task to the broader application scenario in which they are placed.

Attention sinks should generally be managed as a distinct object even when a sink is an indispensable bias, rescaling factor, semantic carrier, or information aggregator rather than an uninformative numerical reservoir.

Every method placed in the attention-redistribution branch reallocates probability mass while preserving the attention-row total, despite the branch also containing post-Softmax sink attenuation and head-pattern broadcasting that do not satisfy that invariant.

techniques.role: Separates fixed, moving, textual, visual, expert-routed, and diffusion-model manifestations before applying the common sink label.
Formalizes one source-derived detector as cumulative received attention above tau times the global mean.
Classifies utilization by whether a system retains, reallocates, creates, or reuses sink behavior.
Distinguishes high attention probabilities from small value states and near-no-op output contributions.
Links aligned weight, activation, and attention outliers across layers as a proposed numerical pathway.
Treats sink-token A-times-V contributions that remain similar across queries as an implicit attention-output bias.
Uses positional decomposition and cosine geometry to characterize sink tokens as stable reference points.
Groups gates, dummy denominator mass, and learnable bias as controllable alternatives to softmax offloading onto a real token.
Groups modified attention normalization, optimizer/loss/norm changes, and value-path interventions by the link they aim to disrupt.
Maps the literature to nine deployment and analysis scenarios as a qualitative selection guide.
Annotates cited studies by utilization, interpretation, mitigation, application, venue, and year in Appendix A.
Reviewer-side check that reconciles counts, definitions, equations, and source versions rather than accepting the survey abstractions verbatim.

evaluations.setting: Survey-level corpus and taxonomy accounting across the 103-page arXiv v2 paper: PDF pp.6-7 Section 1.2, p.73 Sections 8-9, pp.74-85 Appendix A, and pp.86-103 References.
evaluations.metric: Claimed study count, Appendix table rows, unique bracketed study IDs, and number of taxonomy branches.
evaluations.result: The paper variously reports over 210, over 200, and over 180 studies; Figure 3 reports 206. A reviewer recount finds 222 Appendix rows but 208 unique reference IDs, organized under 4 utilization branches, 4 named interpretation branches plus an additional-theories bucket, 4 named mitigation branches plus an additional-techniques bucket, and 9 application scenarios.
evaluations.baseline: The author-claimed absence of an earlier comprehensive attention-sink survey; there is no documented systematic-review protocol or independent corpus baseline.

evaluations.setting: Temporal literature trend from January 2023 through January 2026 in survey PDF p.6 Section 1.2, Figure 3.
evaluations.metric: Cumulative publication count and final count by Fundamental Utilization, Mechanistic Interpretation, and Strategic Mitigation.
evaluations.result: The plotted totals are 39 near October 2023, 107 near October 2024, 186 near October 2025, and 206 in January 2026; the final stack is 106 utilization, 68 interpretation, and 32 mitigation.
evaluations.baseline: Earlier plotted dates in the same author-coded tally; no search database, category coding rule, uncertainty, or multi-label handling is reported.

evaluations.setting: Generic attention-sink identification in a length-L attention matrix in survey PDF p.10 Section 2.2.2, Equation 5.
evaluations.metric: Cumulative received attention A-hat_j relative to the mean cumulative attention mu_A, with token j marked when A-hat_j exceeds tau times mu_A.
evaluations.result: The survey cites tau=1000 as an example and separately cites the first token receiving the maximum attention in 98% of heads for selected LLMs.
evaluations.baseline: Global mean cumulative attention across tokens; these are inherited source results, not a detector evaluated by the survey across its claimed architecture scope.

evaluations.setting: Reviewer algebra check of the survey's unified attention-redistribution abstraction in PDF p.25 Section 3.2.1 Equation 20 and p.27 Section 3.2.2 Equations 22-23.
evaluations.metric: Whether each named redistribution operation conserves a normalized attention row's total probability mass and transfers removed sink mass to another token set.
evaluations.result: Equation 20 conserves mass only under alpha+beta=1. Equation 22 explicitly takes alpha<1 and beta=0 while leaving non-sinks unchanged, so a row with sink mass m sums to 1-(1-alpha)m<1 rather than one. Equation 23 broadcasts one head's entire pattern to other heads and therefore performs replacement, not within-row transfer. At least two named members violate the branch's defining operation.
evaluations.baseline: The paper's own page-25 requirement that redistribution attenuate sinks, assign the freed mass to target tokens, and preserve total attention mass.

evaluations.setting: StreamingLLM sink-plus-recent-token KV caching discussed in survey PDF p.22 Section 3.1.2 and checked against official arxiv:2309.17453v4 for the Llama-2, MPT, Falcon, and Pythia setting.
evaluations.metric: Stable language modeling context length and streaming inference speed.
evaluations.result: The underlying paper reports stable operation to 4 million or more tokens and up to 22.2x speedup.
evaluations.baseline: Sliding-window recomputation without permanent initial sink KVs; the survey reuses this primary result and performs no replication or pooled comparison.

evaluations.setting: MInference pattern-specific sparse prefill with enforced sink visibility in survey PDF p.23 Section 3.1.2, Equation 16 and Figure 14.
evaluations.metric: Prefill speedup and task accuracy relative to dense attention.
evaluations.result: The survey reports up to 10x acceleration without accuracy loss.
evaluations.baseline: Full/dense prefill in the cited MInference study; no common hardware, model, context-length, or accuracy protocol is used to compare this result with other preservation methods.

evaluations.setting: Gated Attention for Large Language Models in survey PDF pp.54-55 Section 5.1.2, Figures 37-38: more than 30 gating variants on 15B MoE and 1.7B dense models trained on 3.5 trillion tokens.
evaluations.metric: Attention share assigned to the initial token, training loss/stability, and qualitative long-context performance.
evaluations.result: Head-specific post-SDPA sigmoid gating reduces mean first-token attention across layers from 46.7% to 4.8%; in layer 21 the illustrated reduction is 83% to 4%. The survey says post-SDPA head-wise gating offers the best effectiveness-efficiency trade-off.
evaluations.baseline: Ungated softmax attention and alternative gate positions/forms in the cited study; no direct survey comparison with modified Softmax, explicit bias, or pre-training interventions.

evaluations.setting: Modified-Softmax evidence inherited from separate Softmax-1 and Softpick studies in survey PDF pp.58-59 Section 5.2.2, Figures 40-41, rather than run in one shared experiment.
evaluations.metric: First-token attention, sink rate, hidden-state activation kurtosis, sparsity, and quantized performance.
evaluations.result: The survey reports Softmax-1 reducing first-token attention from 65% to 3.3% and activation kurtosis from 1657 to 3.1; for a 340M Softpick model it reports 0% sink rate, kurtosis 33,510 to 340, and 46.97% sparse attention in the cited source.
evaluations.baseline: Standard Softmax within each separate source study; model sizes, data, training recipes, sink definitions, and quantization settings differ, so the numbers do not rank the methods.

evaluations.setting: Outlier-Safe Pre-Training synthesis in survey PDF pp.63-65 Section 5.4.2 and Figure 42, combining Muon, single-scale RMSNorm, and an embedding projection.
evaluations.metric: Presence of extreme activation outliers, training scale, and low-bit robustness.
evaluations.result: The survey reports validation on a 1.4B model trained on 1 trillion tokens and calls it the first production-scale LLM without extreme activation outliers; Figure 42 separately visualizes 1.4B runs at 100B tokens for Adam, Muon, and the full framework.
evaluations.baseline: Adam and Muon-only training in the cited work; the survey does not report a shared attention-sink metric proving that removal of activation outliers equals removal of every sink phenotype.

evaluations.setting: Cross-architecture evidence used to motivate one definition in survey PDF p.18 Section 2.5 and p.20 Section 2.6, including diffusion transformers and vision-language-action models.
evaluations.metric: CLIP text-image alignment, perceptual shift relative to random masking, and real-world robotic manipulation performance.
evaluations.result: The survey reports that suppressing DiT sinks leaves CLIP-T alignment unchanged but produces a perceptual shift about six times random masking, while repurposed ViT registers improve RetoVLA real-world manipulation by 17.1%.
evaluations.baseline: Random token masking for the DiT causal analysis and the original VLA without register reuse; these task-specific results are inherited and undermine a universal interpretation of sinks as low-information no-ops.

evaluations.setting: No survey-authored controlled evaluation in the contribution list at PDF p.7 Section 1.2, the author limitations at p.73 Section 9, or the study table at pp.74-85 Appendix A.
evaluations.metric: New experiments, pooled estimates, standardized benchmark comparisons, formal theorem, review search reproducibility, and evidence-quality scoring.
evaluations.result: None are provided. All model-performance numbers are selected from cited primary studies, while the survey's own outputs are taxonomy, narrative synthesis, equations, a publication plot, application mapping, and the Appendix table.
evaluations.baseline: A systematic review or benchmark would preregister search and screening, reconcile study counts, code evidence quality, and compare methods under common definitions and budgets; this paper does not.

limitations: [Author-stated, p.73 Section 9] Coverage centers on well-established CLMs, dense and MoE LLMs, MLLMs, and ViTs; hybrid-linear attention, VGGT, and other emerging or specialized transformer families are not comprehensive because the literature is sparse.
[Author-stated, pp.24 and 28] Fixed sink positions are cheap but miss non-initial or dynamic sinks; dynamic detection adds computation and conflicts with optimized attention kernels.

[Author-stated, pp.39, 44, 47, and 71-72] Training dynamics behind value suppression, aligned outlier circuits, implicit bias formation, and anchor emergence remain incompletely formalized, and much geometric evidence is correlational.

[Author-stated, pp.56-66 and 71-72] Gating, modified Softmax, learnable bias, and most pre-training interventions generally require training from scratch; parameter-efficient post-hoc adaptation is largely missing.
[Author-stated, pp.56, 60, and 71] Gates, post-Softmax redistribution, dynamic detectors, and nonstandard normalizers introduce latency, parameters, or fused-kernel incompatibility.

[Author-stated, pp.56, 62, and 72] The field lacks a standardized benchmark for sink elimination, outlier suppression, utility, computational overhead, and parameter cost, preventing fair method comparison.
[Author-stated, p.72] Cross-architecture and cross-modal transfer is rarely tested, and combinations of handling techniques are mostly studied in isolation.

[Reviewer-inferred] The review has no database/search strategy, inclusion or exclusion criteria, time cutoff, screening flow, deduplication rule, source-quality appraisal, coder agreement, or protocol for updates, so comprehensiveness and the first-survey claim are not reproducible.
[Reviewer-inferred] Corpus accounting is inconsistent: over 210, over 200, over 180, Figure 3's 206, Appendix A's 208 unique study IDs, and 245 total references are never reconciled.

[Reviewer-inferred] The definition conflates at least four functional kinds: null/no-op reservoirs, implicit bias or rescaling tokens, semantic/global information hubs, and merely high-attention geometric anchors.

[Reviewer-inferred] The survey often converts evidence from a specific model, data scale, layer, head, or task into architecture-wide language without effect sizes, variance, negative cases, or a risk-of-bias assessment.

[Reviewer-inferred] Architecture-changing interventions such as gating or replacing Softmax alter expressivity, gradients, sparsity, and optimization in addition to sink behavior; downstream gains therefore do not isolate the sink as mediator.

[Reviewer-inferred] The attention-redistribution taxonomy violates its stated mass-preservation invariant: Equation 22 deletes post-Softmax mass and Equation 23 replaces head patterns, so comparisons inside the branch conflate redistribution, attenuation/gating, and head replacement.

[Reviewer-inferred] Equation 31 mistranscribes FOCUS's attraction loss with the wrong sign and aggregation, demonstrating that the paper's many source-level equations cannot be assumed implementation-faithful without primary-source checking.

[Reviewer-inferred] The current direct study arxiv:2504.03889v4 is omitted: it finds attention-weight sink scores alone miss more than 7% of inactive heads on average, negative evidence against using sink attention as a sufficient head-importance signal.
[Reviewer-inferred] Figure 3 stops at January 2026 while the v2 appendix contains papers through May 2026; the time-series total and current-paper table therefore use different implicit cutoffs.

[Reviewer-inferred] The author limitation section mentions only architecture coverage and does not acknowledge the absent review protocol, inconsistent counts, heterogeneous evidence, or lack of new validation.
failure_modes: A fixed first-token cache policy fails when sinks emerge on delimiters, later tokens, visual patches, different layers, or moving diffusion-model positions.
A detector based only on cumulative attention can flag task-relevant hubs or miss heads whose low output contribution is caused by values rather than an extreme attention pattern.
Post-Softmax redistribution may remove a functional bias, rescaling route, semantic carrier, or anti-overmixing anchor and thereby improve a sink metric while degrading model utility.
Redistribution and dynamic scoring can materialize attention matrices, defeating FlashAttention-style kernels and erasing the efficiency gain the method was intended to provide.
Learned registers can relocate rather than eliminate the sink, can aggregate information that makes them semantically important, and require tuning of token count and placement.
Modified attention normalizers may flatten genuinely necessary sharp attention, require retraining, or lose compatibility with established kernels and checkpoints.
Clipping outliers without preserving their bias or rescaling function can destabilize training or reduce accuracy; outlier removal is not automatically sink-safe mitigation.
Gated attention can add non-negligible latency or parameters, and the gate may suppress useful updates if transferred outside its training regime.
Cross-modal background heuristics can treat an apparently low-information patch as dispensable even when it carries global scene, spatial, or conditioning information.
Quantizing low-magnitude sink values can create disproportionate relative error even though the unquantized A-times-V contribution is small.
A method selected from the scenario guidelines can fail because reported gains use a different sink definition, model size, task metric, context length, precision, or hardware budget.
Security systems can exploit stable high-attention positions as stealthy backdoor or hallucination-attack gateways, while a defense that assumes static locations remains bypassable.
Treating correlation between outlier magnitude, geometry, and attention as a complete circuit can misidentify downstream correlates as causes and motivate the wrong intervention.

Implementing Equation 22 as though it were normalized redistribution silently scales down the entire attention-head update; subsequent residual and normalization behavior can then drive an apparent gain that is not attributable to where attention was reallocated.
Unverified survey equations can reverse an optimization objective, as Equation 31 does for FOCUS, causing an implementation based on the survey rather than the source to behave oppositely.
reusable_insights: Always report attention probability, value norm, and the norm or direction of the final attention contribution together; high A with near-zero V is not the same object as a high-contribution information hub.

Describe a sink intervention by its functional verb—preserve, redistribute, create, repurpose, substitute, or remove—because methods with the same sink-rate effect can have opposite assumptions about sink utility.
Treat the softmax simplex as lacking an explicit null route; a gate, dummy denominator mass, or explicit bias can supply that route without forcing probability onto a real token.
Track sink identity per input, layer, head, training checkpoint, and modality rather than assuming the first token is a static global sink.
Separate null sinks, bias/rescaling sinks, semantic aggregation hubs, and geometric anchors before comparing methods or claiming cross-architecture generality.
Use causal interventions that preserve all other computations where possible; if architecture or optimizer changes, test mediation by restoring the removed sink function explicitly.
Evaluate handling methods on a joint frontier of utility, sink rate, output contribution, activation range, quantized quality, latency, memory, parameter cost, and kernel compatibility.
For pretrained deployment, prioritize reversible preservation or carefully validated calibration; gates, bias, new normalizers, and pre-training recipes solve a different greenfield design problem.
Registers often control the location of an internal computation rather than eliminate it; evaluate what the register encodes before discarding it.
A field taxonomy should publish its search, cutoff, deduplication, coding, and multi-label rules so publication trends and coverage counts can be reconstructed.

Define taxonomy branches by checkable invariants: distinguish mass-conserving within-row redistribution from post-Softmax attenuation, logit rebiasing followed by renormalization, and cross-head pattern replacement.
Source-level formulas need spot checks against official primary versions, especially when a survey rewrites diverse methods into a common notation.
Negative evidence such as attention-based inactive-head scores missing output-inactive heads is essential for calibrating attention-sink metrics and avoiding attention-is-explanation errors.
open_questions: What operational definition separates a low-information no-op sink from a semantic information hub, an implicit bias token, a rescaling outlier, and a geometric anchor across modalities?
Can a length-, layer-, head-, and architecture-normalized sink metric predict causal output contribution better than cumulative attention alone?
When during pre-training do weight, residual, value, and attention outliers align, and which link in that lifecycle is necessary for sink formation?
Does explicitly restoring a removed sink's null, bias, rescaling, or anti-overmixing function rescue performance after ablation, thereby distinguishing competing mechanisms?
Which sink phenotypes are beneficial, neutral, or harmful under language modeling, reasoning, retrieval, vision, diffusion, multimodal grounding, and safety objectives?
Can dynamic non-initial sink detection be implemented without materializing post-Softmax scores or breaking fused attention kernels?
Can pretrained models acquire gates, dummy bias mass, or modified normalization through low-rank/adaptor updates rather than full retraining, and what functionality is lost?
How do sink behaviors change with grouped-query attention, MoE routing, linear/hybrid attention, state-space components, and 3D or streaming world models?
What standardized benchmark should jointly measure sink identity, A-times-V contribution, model utility, quantized robustness, latency, memory, and parameter overhead?
How robust are sink-based backdoors and sink-based defenses when an adversary moves the sink across positions, layers, modalities, or tokenization schemes?
Do combinations such as explicit null bias plus gated rescaling or preservation plus dynamic calibration provide complementary gains, or do they redundantly suppress the same function?
Can the survey corpus be reconstructed with documented queries, independent coding, consistent cutoffs, study-quality labels, and a reconciled unique-paper count?

Which reported redistribution gains survive after separating probability-preserving reallocation from attention-output attenuation, logit rebiasing, and cross-head pattern replacement under a common model and compute budget?
How often do survey-level method abstractions contain sign, normalization, or setting errors when compared with current official source versions?
Does a low attention-sink score meaningfully imply an active or useful head, given evidence that attention-only scores miss output-inactive heads?

competitive_landscape.title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
competitive_landscape.difference: This paper introduced the named causal-LLM attention-sink phenomenon in the streaming/KV-cache setting and tested sink-plus-window retention to at least 4 million tokens with up to 22.2x speedup; the survey generalizes that concrete phenomenon into a cross-architecture taxonomy without adding a streaming experiment.

competitive_landscape.title: Quantizable Transformers: Removing Outliers by Helping Attention Heads Do Nothing
competitive_landscape.difference: This work predates the named StreamingLLM sink paper but directly connects outliers to heads implementing no-op updates and tests clipped Softmax and gated attention on BERT, OPT, and ViT; the survey elevates its account to one main mechanism branch but does not re-test its causal scope.

competitive_landscape.title: Massive Activations in Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: This paper characterizes rare massive activations, their input-stable bias role, and their concentration of attention in LLMs and ViTs; the survey distributes those results across outlier circuits and implicit attention bias rather than contributing new activation measurements.

competitive_landscape.title: When Attention Sink Emerges in Language Models: An Empirical View
competitive_landscape.difference: This controlled empirical study varies optimization, data, objective, and attention operations up to 1B parameters and interprets sinks as key biases; the survey summarizes its conclusions but still identifies training dynamics as unresolved and supplies no longitudinal experiment of its own.

competitive_landscape.title: Active-Dormant Attention Heads: Mechanistically Demystifying Extreme-Token Phenomena in LLMs
competitive_landscape.difference: This paper derives mutual reinforcement on a one-to-three-layer Bigram-Backcopy task and checks predicted extreme-token properties in Llama and OLMo; the survey places it among additional theories but does not distinguish toy-task proof from large-model correlation in its top-level synthesis.

competitive_landscape.title: Vision Transformers Need Registers
competitive_landscape.difference: This study identifies high-norm background artifacts and tests learned register tokens in supervised and self-supervised ViTs; the survey treats those artifacts as visual attention sinks and register insertion as learnable-prefix utilization, a broader label not established by the original abstract alone.

competitive_landscape.title: Softpick: No Attention Sink, No Massive Activations with Rectified Softmax
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct mitigation and closest metric antecedent
competitive_landscape.difference: Softpick directly tests a non-sum-to-one rectified attention rule and reports 0% sink rate, sparse maps, lower kurtosis, and quantization gains on 340M and 1.8B models in current v4; the survey cites selected results but provides no head-to-head normalization against other mitigation families.

competitive_landscape.title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free
competitive_landscape.difference: This paper compares more than 30 gate variants on 15B MoE and 1.7B dense models trained on 3.5T tokens and isolates post-SDPA head gating as effective; the survey uses it as central mitigation evidence but cannot generalize its cost or benefits to ViTs and MLLMs without cross-architecture trials.

competitive_landscape.title: Attention Sinks Are Provably Necessary in Softmax Transformers: Evidence from Trigger-Conditional Tasks
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct necessity-theory antecedent and boundary case
competitive_landscape.difference: This work proves sink necessity for a specific trigger-conditional task under normalized Softmax and shows ReLU attention avoids it; it supports the survey's normalization story only under explicit conditions, whereas the survey's language about inevitable emergence across transformers is broader than the theorem.

competitive_landscape.title: A Unified View of Attention and Residual Sinks: Outlier-Driven Rescaling is Essential for Transformer Training
competitive_landscape.difference: This paper argues attention and residual outliers jointly rescale non-outlier components and that clipping them can hurt stability, while explicit gated rescaling preserves function; the survey includes the theory but its generic mitigation framing can still imply that sink removal itself is the goal.

competitive_landscape.title: Identifying and Evaluating Inactive Heads in Pretrained LLMs
competitive_landscape.difference: Current v4 evaluates 12 head-inactivity scores across three model families and finds attention-sink scores alone miss more than 7% of inactive heads on average, while output-norm scores identify over 12% inactive heads; the survey does not cite this direct warning against treating sink attention as a sufficient importance measure.

competitive_landscape.title: FOCUS: Fused Observation of Channels for Unveiling Spectra
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct learned-sink application antecedent and source-audit record
competitive_landscape.difference: FOCUS v2 trains a [SINK] token with a negative mean-attention attraction term over selected heads and reports less than 1% parameters on hyperspectral ViT interpretation; the survey's Equation 31 replaces that objective with a positive squared norm whose minimization has the opposite direction.

competitive_landscape.title: A Mechanistic Account of Attention Sinks in GPT-2: One Circuit, Broader Implications for Mitigation
competitive_landscape.difference: Ran-Milo et al. combine structural analysis with causal interventions to identify a GPT-2 sink circuit involving learned query bias, the first-layer MLP's transformation of position, and key projection structure. Crucially, each component is individually dispensable in architectures that still form sinks, directly supporting the survey's plural-mechanism caution while limiting any inference that its proposed levels constitute one architecture-invariant circuit.

competitive_landscape.title: The Spike, the Sparse and the Sink: Anatomy of Massive Activations and Attention Sinks
competitive_landscape.difference: Sun et al. experimentally distinguish massive activations as global implicit-parameter-like signals from attention sinks as local, head-specific short-range biases, and report that changing pre-norm causes the phenomena to decouple. This is stronger primary evidence than a simple causal chain from activation outlier to sink and reinforces the need to phenotype the two quantities separately.

competitive_landscape.title: When Do Attention Circuits Form? Developmental Trajectories of Capability and Attention-Sink Emergence Across Three 1B-Class Architectures
competitive_landscape.difference: Xu tracks 10 checkpoints in each of Pythia 1B, OLMo 1B, and OLMoE 1B-7B and reports gradual versus abrupt BOS-attractor trajectories, plus a 10-20x token separation between induction-circuit and sink formation in the DCLM models. As a single current study it is not a general resolution, but it supplies exactly the checkpoint-level, cross-architecture evidence the survey identifies as missing and argues against one universal emergence schedule.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first comprehensive and systematic survey of attention-sink research, a novel Utilization-Interpretation-Mitigation taxonomy, in-depth methodological synthesis, critical future directions, and a nine-scenario application map, accompanied by a maintained paper repository.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper spans 103 pages, organizes manifestations across major transformer families, develops three main analytical dimensions with explicit sub-taxonomies, gives a publication trend and a 12-page tagged study table, and no earlier dedicated attention-sink survey appeared in the official primary records returned by the reviewer's exact-title and mechanism searches. However, the paper gives no search protocol that could establish exhaustiveness or priority.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is organizational: a broad cross-architecture compendium and a memorable three-axis taxonomy assembled from direct antecedents. The mechanisms, mitigation techniques, equations, and empirical numbers are prior-work contributions, not new evidence. The first-systematic-survey wording should be narrowed to a plausible first dedicated narrative survey among the checked records because corpus counts conflict, inclusion is unreproducible, one direct negative-evidence study is omitted, and a spot check found a sign-level equation error.

reviewer_notes: Read the pinned 103-page extraction end to end, including Appendix A and all 245 references, and visually checked the pinned PDF on pages 5, 6, 10, 21, 31, 36, 53, 73, and 74 for the taxonomy tree, Figure 3 counts, Equation 5, section boxes, Equation 31, conclusion/limitations, and table layout. The source is arXiv v2 (official arXiv history: revised 2026-06-05); the indexed PDF hash 9983b4652ad435d90b5bf557a7ae3b879467673e51e6c7fac2236525e52dbbeb is byte-identical to the exact official https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.10098v2 endpoint, and the extraction is pinned to the index hashes and 2026-08-23 timestamp above. An independent secondary verification on 2026-08-23 re-read all 103 pages, re-rendered the decisive equations, figures, and table boundaries, and rechecked every competitor against the current primary record. Exact-source queries were run on 2026-08-23 in three required families: (1) mechanism+task (attention sink streaming/KV cache, no-op/outlier/implicit bias, ViT registers, active-dormant and necessity theory); (2) closest evaluation/baseline (sink rate, first-token attention, quantization kurtosis, gated and rectified/non-normalized attention); and (3) novelty/cited predecessor (exact survey title, first-survey language, StreamingLLM, Quantizable Transformers, Massive Activations, When Attention Sink Emerges). Official arXiv records checked were 2309.17453v4, 2306.12929v2, 2402.17762v2, 2410.10781v2, 2410.13835v2, 2309.16588v2, 2504.20966v4, 2505.06708v1, 2603.11487v5, 2601.22966v1, 2504.03889v4, and 2507.14787v2; official OpenReview/proceedings pages were also used to corroborate the ICLR/NeurIPS records where available. No earlier dedicated attention-sink survey was found in those official searches, but absence cannot prove priority without a documented systematic search. The reviewer recounted Appendix A from the pinned extraction: 222 paper rows, 208 unique bracketed IDs, and repeated IDs 27, 30, 43, 45, 46, 47, 54, 64, 66, 94, 205, 213, and 227. This explains row duplication but not the paper's incompatible over-210, over-200, over-180, and 206 totals. A direct source check of FOCUS v2 found its actual attraction objective is -lambda times mean attention to the sink over selected layers/heads; survey Equation 31's positive squared norm is not equivalent. arxiv:2504.03889v4 was not found anywhere in the survey text or references and supplies relevant negative evidence: attention-weight sink scores underestimate inactive heads relative to output-norm interventions. No new experiment is attributed to this survey. Confidence is high for the pinned text, taxonomy, displayed numbers, count audit, and source-version checks; lower for exhaustiveness/priority and for causal generalizations inherited from heterogeneous cited studies.
